concept_name: Hydrogen Bonding — Why Water Boils Far Higher Than Expected
section: Class 11 Chemistry Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.9 — Hydrogen Bonding
source_book: NCERT Chemistry Class 11, Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.9 — chapter-index scope reference only; teaching, sequence, examples and phrasing authored from first principles. NCERT Exemplar consulted for misconception beliefs only (a hydrogen bond behaves like a covalent bond; boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen); no problem text, figure or prose imported. Desk 1, concept 2 of 2 in the Phase-0 bonding wave, on the bonding_scene scenario (field_3d, scenario capabilities E1 + E2).

real_world_anchor.primary: Water boils at the same temperature everywhere on Earth at sea level, and by its own molecular family it should boil near 180 kelvin — there would be no liquid water, no oceans. The 193-kelvin gap between that prediction and water's real boiling point exists only because water's hydrogen bonds have to be broken first.
real_world_anchor.secondary: Boiling water never splits it into hydrogen and oxygen — the steam above a cooking pot is still H2O. Only the weak links between molecules break; the covalent O-H bonds inside each molecule never do.

delta_chi.name: electronegativity difference between H and the bonded atom

donor_charge.name: partial positive charge on the donor hydrogen
donor_charge.note: H2O +0.319 - H2S +0.036 - H2Se +0.030 - H2Te -0.003 (no donor). Donor threshold 0.15.

acceptor_charge.name: partial negative charge on the acceptor atom
acceptor_charge.note: H2O O -0.638 - H2S S -0.071 - H2Se Se -0.060 - H2Te Te +0.003. Acceptor threshold 0.30, so {N,O,F} emerges from the thresholds — never a whitelist.

E_hbond.name: hydrogen-bond dissociation energy (tabulated mean, published)
E_hbond.note: STATE_3 formula surface. Tabulated mean bond enthalpy convention. Sits inside NCERT §4.9's own 10-40 kJ.mol-1 band for hydrogen bonds.

E_OH.name: O-H covalent bond dissociation energy (tabulated mean, published)

H_link_pm.name: H...O hydrogen-bond distance
H_link_pm.note: forms at H...O <= 210 pm, breaks at H...O >= 260 pm (hysteresis); measured linear bond 180.0 pm at 179.9 degrees at the authored 5.75-unit separation

links_per_unit.name: mean hydrogen-bond links per molecule (mean degree, 2L/N)
links_per_unit.note: 298 K mean 3.40 (range 3.19-3.59, 640 ms time-averaged) - 600 K mean 2.85 (range 2.59-3.16). NEVER multiply this figure directly by E_hbond — only half of it is owned per molecule (the mean degree, F9 guard).

T_K.note: live on STATE_6 (scripted ramp 298 to 600, drag-seized) and STATE_8 (all core); static 298 elsewhere

count.name: number of water molecules in the network
count.note: live on STATE_5 and STATE_8 only; centre-outward growth, shrinking never moves a survivor

boiling_point.name: boiling point of the displayed species

formulas.hbond_link_criterion: forms when H...O <= 210 pm AND donor_charge >= 0.15 AND acceptor_charge >= 0.30 AND D-H...A angle within the 40 degree window; breaks at H...O >= 260 pm (hysteresis)
formulas.links_per_unit: 2 * L / N  (L = total links, N = molecule count — the mean DEGREE, not links owned per molecule)
formulas.boiling_trend: least-squares fit of (period_x, boiling_point_y) over {H2S, H2Se, H2Te}; water's y-value minus the fitted line's value at water's x = the gap

links_per_unit.formula: links_per_unit = 2 * L / N, time-averaged over the engine's 640 ms lookback

boiling_point.formula: boiling_trend = least-squares fit of (period, boiling_point) over {H2S, H2Se, H2Te}; gap = actual water boiling point - fitted value at water's period

constraints: the O-H covalent bond length is invariant under every authored motion in this concept — no intra-unit bond-break machinery exists anywhere in bonding_scene

the hydrogen-bond link criterion depends only on donor/acceptor partial-charge thresholds (donor >= 0.15, acceptor >= 0.30) crossed by whatever species is on screen — never a hardcoded element whitelist
a hydrogen bond forms at H...O <= 210 pm and breaks at H...O >= 260 pm — hysteresis, not a single threshold
links_per_unit = 2L/N is the mean DEGREE; only half that figure (about 1.70 at 298 K) is 'owned' per molecule — never multiply links_per_unit directly by E_hbond
electronegativity differences and derived partial charges are fixed per species (Pauling scale) — independent of the temperature or count sliders

no chemical reaction, state symbol, oxidation number, or mole-scale factor appears anywhere in this concept — every species shown is a single stable molecule, never transformed into another substance; STATE_4's H2O to H2S swap is a scripted scene-wide substitution for teaching, narrated as 'swap', never 'react'

concept_tier_note: Tier: diamond, capabilities 1 + 4. A whiteboard draws two water molecules and one dotted line. It cannot show thirty molecules making and breaking links continuously (capability 1), and it cannot make the boiling-point anomaly emerge — the trend line extrapolated from H2S/H2Se/H2Te with water landing 193 K above it, the engine deriving the gap by least squares rather than the author asserting it (capability 4).

aha_moment.statement: Water should boil near 180 K, but it boils at 373 because of hydrogen bonds.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The boiling-point trend line, fitted through hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen selenide and hydrogen telluride, is drawn out to 180 K while water's own point sits 193 K above it.

STATE_1.title: Hydrogen becomes an almost bare proton
STATE_1.label: Water: the shared electron pair slides toward oxygen, leaving hydrogen almost bare

tts_sentences.text_en: Oxygen pulls the shared electron pair much harder than hydrogen.
Watch the pair slide toward oxygen.
Hydrogen has no other electrons, so what remains is an almost bare, positive proton: delta plus, oxygen delta minus.
The electronegativity difference is 1.24.

STATE_2.title: A second molecule attaches
STATE_2.label: A second water molecule turns and settles into a hydrogen bond, 180 picometres from the first

tts_sentences.text_en: The delta-plus hydrogen attracts the delta-minus oxygen of a second water molecule.
The second molecule turns and settles in a straight line: hydrogen to oxygen, 180 picometres — almost twice the 96-picometre O–H bond inside each molecule, and a dashed link forms.
This is a hydrogen bond.

STATE_3.title: The weak link breaks first
STATE_3.label: Pull the two molecules apart: the dashed link breaks near 260 picometres while both O–H bonds stay unchanged

tts_sentences.text_en: Pull the two molecules apart.
The dashed link stretches until it fails — both O–H bonds are unchanged.
A hydrogen bond takes about 20 kilojoules per mole to break; a covalent O–H bond takes 464.
This link is more than twenty times weaker.

misconception_watch.belief: A hydrogen bond is a bond like any other — as strong and as permanent as a covalent bond.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The dashed link is given its honest evidence first (it forms at 180 pm and holds through the previous state), then breaks under the pull while both solid O–H sticks stay byte-identical throughout; the formula surface lands the 20 versus 464 kJ.mol-1 scale in the same beat.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: A hydrogen bond takes about 20 kilojoules per mole to break; a covalent O–H bond takes 464. This link is more than twenty times weaker.

STATE_4.title: Sulfur is not negative enough
STATE_4.label: Swap oxygen for sulfur: the electronegativity difference collapses and no link forms

tts_sentences.text_en: Swap oxygen for sulfur.
Sulfur pulls only slightly harder than hydrogen — the electronegativity difference falls from 1.24 to 0.38, and the small charges fall with it.
No link forms.
A hydrogen bond needs a strongly negative partner: in practice nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.

STATE_5.title: Links form and break everywhere
STATE_5.label: Thirty water molecules: dashed hydrogen-bond links form and break in every direction, all at once

tts_sentences.text_en: Now thirty water molecules.
Each delta-plus hydrogen can link to a delta-minus oxygen on a neighbour, so dashed links form in every direction — and they keep breaking and re-forming as the molecules move.
On average, each molecule holds more than three links at any moment.

STATE_6.title: Heat breaks links, not bonds
STATE_6.label: Heat the network: the jiggle grows harder and the averaged link count falls, while every O–H bond stays intact

tts_sentences.text_en: Heat the network.
Every molecule jiggles harder, and the average number of links each one holds falls.
Not one O–H bond breaks.
Heat weakens the hydrogen bonds between molecules; it never breaks the covalent bonds inside them.

misconception_watch.belief: Boiling water breaks its O–H bonds — boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: Heating raises the jiggle amplitude and lowers the averaged link count live on the HUD, while every O–H stick in every one of the thirty molecules stays pixel-identical through the entire ramp — the engine has no machinery to break a bond inside a molecule.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Not one O–H bond breaks. Heat weakens the hydrogen bonds between molecules; it never breaks the covalent bonds inside them.

STATE_7.title: Water boils far higher than expected
STATE_7.label: Compare water's boiling point with its own molecular family — the 193-kelvin gap is the hydrogen bonds

tts_sentences.text_en: Compare water's family: hydrogen sulfide 213 kelvin, hydrogen selenide 232, hydrogen telluride 271.
The trend predicts water near 180 kelvin, yet it boils at 373 kelvin, one hundred degrees Celsius.
That 193-kelvin gap is there because those hydrogen bonds have to be broken first.
Without them, Earth would have no oceans.

regeneration_variants.label: Same weak-link-versus-strong-bond reasoning, ammonia's lone pair instead of water's
regeneration_variants.physical_world: Ammonia's nitrogen carries a lone pair and forms hydrogen bonds to neighbouring ammonia molecules, the same donor-hydrogen-to-electronegative-acceptor link seen in water — weaker than any covalent N-H bond, and constantly breaking and re-forming in liquid ammonia.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical donor/acceptor partial-charge threshold reasoning and the same order-of-magnitude weak-link-versus-strong-bond contrast; the taught relationship (a strongly electronegative acceptor is required, and the resulting link is far weaker than a covalent bond) is unchanged.
